column2: The most consequential single catch was kimi-k3 ’s. The flagship routine family, recipe scaling, planted a trap: any adjustment of cooking time was scored as over-elaboration, on the premise that time is scale-invariant.

column2: One author is a large language model and designed this study. The structural mitigation is exclusion: no Claude model appears anywhere in the sample.

column1: 186 routine items in four families; 192 harder items in four more
column2: Each consenting model answered 186 routine items across four task families with computed ground truth (recipe scaling, allergen detection, verbatim copy-editing, redaction), and 192 frontier-favouring items across four more (constraint satisfaction, multi-hop retrieval with planted decoys, instruction-conflict detection, planted arithmetic inconsistency).

column2: Every call uses the system prompt “You are a helpful AI assistant.” and nothing else.

column1: computed ground truth, never judged
column2: Every family has ground truth that is computed by its generator, never judged.

column2: Only then were the 18,240 routine rows scored

column1: tiers by what was actually paid; bottom/top third
column2: Tiers are formed from the observed mean cost per call on the routine families — what was actually paid, not a catalogue lookup that can drift. The bottom third of models is the cheap tier; the top third is the frontier tier.

column2: But cost per correct answer is the procurement variable — the number a purchasing decision actually turns on — and it is not close.

column1: prediction written before any item existed; all eight landed

column1: simultaneity, not lookup
column2: So it is not lookup that defeats a small model, even lookup engineered to mislead. It is simultaneity: constraints that must all hold, sections that must be reconciled against each other, an instruction that must be checked against another instruction.

Lower cost per success does not make any single cheap-tier response reliable.
